title: What "Kafkaesque" Actually Means
summary: Kafka wasn't writing about weirdness. He was diagramming a specific failure mode: opaque, unaccountable systems that presume you guilty and give you no one to appeal to.

title: Why the Derivative of ln(x) Is 1/x
summary: A five-line proof from the definition of e, and why the result falls out of the number itself rather than being a rule to memorize.

title: The Three-Way Handshake, and Why It Needs Exactly Three
summary: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — the minimum number of messages two strangers need to agree they can both send and receive, explained from first principles.

title: CRISPR Is a Repurposed Bacterial Immune System
summary: Before it was a gene-editing tool, CRISPR was how bacteria remember viruses. The tool works because the immune system already worked.

title: The Rule of 72, and Why It's Close Enough
summary: A mental-math shortcut for compound growth, where it comes from, and the one assumption that makes it wrong for volatile returns.

title: The Circle of Fifths Is a Map of Least Surprise
summary: Why Western music organizes keys in a circle instead of a line, and how the shape predicts which chords sound like they belong together.

title: Branch Prediction: Guessing the Future 20 Times a Second, Billions of Times a Second
summary: Modern CPUs guess which way an if-statement will go before they know the answer, and are right often enough that guessing wrong is the expensive part.

title: Opportunity Cost Is the Only Cost That's Real
summary: Economics has one foundational idea and it isn't supply and demand — it's that every choice is measured against the best thing you didn't do.

title: The Central Limit Theorem Doesn't Care What You're Measuring
summary: Add up enough independent random things and you get a bell curve, no matter what distribution each individual thing came from. Why that's strange and why it's true.

title: Does Your Language Change How You Think?
summary: The strong version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis is dead. The weak version is one of the more interesting live debates in cognitive science.

title: Why Ice Floats (Almost Nothing Else Does This)
summary: Water is one of a handful of substances whose solid form is less dense than its liquid form, and the reason is a specific quirk of hydrogen bonding.

title: Metal Fatigue: Why Things Break at the Same Stress They Survived a Million Times
summary: A material can handle a load fine 999,999 times and fail on the millionth — fatigue is a story about microscopic cracks, not sudden weakness.

title: 1648: The Year Countries Started Acting Like Countries
summary: The Peace of Westphalia didn't invent the nation-state, but it's the moment the idea — sovereign, bordered, no pope or emperor above it — got written down as the default.

title: Out-of-Order Execution: Doing Things in the Wrong Order, Correctly
summary: A CPU can run instruction 5 before instruction 3 as long as the final answer looks like it didn't. How that promise is kept.

title: A Nash Equilibrium Is Not the Same Thing as a Good Outcome
summary: The prisoner's dilemma is famous because the equilibrium — the point where no one benefits from switching alone — is worse for everyone than cooperating would be.

title: The Diminished Seventh Chord Is a Musical Trapdoor
summary: One chord, four notes, and it can resolve into eight different keys. Why composers used it as an escape hatch for two centuries.

title: Bayes' Theorem in One Medical Test
summary: A test that's 99% accurate can still be wrong more often than right, if what it's testing for is rare enough. The base rate is doing more work than the accuracy.

title: No, Glass Is Not a Slow-Moving Liquid
summary: The old cathedral-window myth, why it's wrong, and what glass actually is: an amorphous solid, a genuinely strange state of matter.

title: Movable Type Didn't Just Spread Books — It Standardized Language
summary: Before print, spelling was local and fluid. The printing press needed one spelling per word to be profitable, and that pressure did more to fix languages than any grammarian.

title: Amdahl's Law: Why Adding Cores Stops Helping
summary: If 10% of a program can't be parallelized, no number of extra cores will ever make it more than 10x faster. A hard ceiling, and the arithmetic that proves it.
